sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the station and the fast God accepts
sections.b: In Similitude 5 Hermas is keeping a "station" (Greek statiōn, from the Latin army word statio, a soldier's watch), a fast day. Lake notes that the word "is not found elsewhere in Greek writers," but Latin writers such as Tertullian use it for "a fixed time for fasting." The Shepherd calls Hermas's fast "useless": God does not want an empty fast, but a life of obedience (Shepherd of Hermas 54:3-5). Then he gives a rule: guard against evil words and desires, eat only bread and water on the fast day, add up what the day's food would have cost, and give it "to a widow or an orphan or someone in need," so that the one who receives prays for you. Such a fast is "a sacrifice" God accepts (56:6-8). The teaching joins Isaiah 58's call for a fast of justice to the early church's fixed fast days (Didache 8:1).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 54:1-5; Shepherd of Hermas 56:5-9; Isaiah 58:3-7; Matthew 6:16-18; Didache 8:1

common: The Shepherd of Hermas calls a fast day a "station," a Latin word that Lake finds in no other Greek writer.
uncommon: The Shepherd of Hermas makes the fast a form of almsgiving: the money saved on food goes to widows, orphans and the needy.

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: buying souls, the elm and the vine
sections.b: The Similitudes of Hermas return again and again to giving. The first parable tells believers, who live in a foreign city, to buy "souls in distress" instead of fields, to visit widows and orphans, and to spend their estates on them (Shepherd of Hermas 50:8-9). The second pictures the rich man as an elm and the poor man as a vine: the elm bears no fruit, but holds up the vine; the rich man supplies the poor man's needs "without hesitating," and the poor man's prayer, which "has great power with God," completes the rich man's poverty toward God. Both become "partners in the righteous work" (51:5-9). The fast of Similitude 5 ends with the day's food money given to the needy (56:7).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 50:8-10; Shepherd of Hermas 51:3-10; Shepherd of Hermas 56:7; James 1:27; 2 Corinthians 8:13-15

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: wealth, business and the drift from the church
sections.b: Hermas, a former slave who had been in business, writes for a Roman church with rich members. His Similitudes warn that the man with many estates in "this city" may deny his law to keep them (Shepherd of Hermas 50:5), that many business dealings bring many sins (53:5-7), and that some "tangled up in business" denied the Lord (74:1-2). The sharpest picture is of believers who "grew rich and became respected among the nations," put on pride and lived with the pagans, keeping the faith without its works (75:1-3). Yet Hermas does not condemn wealth as such: "This is why the Master made you rich: so that you would carry out these services for him" (50:9), and in the parable of the elm and the vine the rich have their place in the church as supporters of the poor (51).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 50:1-11; Shepherd of Hermas 51:1-10; Shepherd of Hermas 53:5-7; Shepherd of Hermas 74:1-3; Shepherd of Hermas 75:1-4; 1 Timothy 6:17-19; James 5:1-6

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the poor are rich in prayer
sections.b: In the parable of the elm and the vine the poor man "is rich in prayer for others and in praise, and his prayer has great power with God" (Shepherd of Hermas 51:5). The rich man, poor toward the Lord, supports him, and the poor man's prayer "is acceptable to the Lord and rich before him" (51:6). The reversal is that of James 2:5 and Luke 12:21, turned into a partnership.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 51:5-9; James 2:5; Luke 12:21; Psalm 34:6

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the slave in the vineyard
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas never uses the names "Jesus" or "Christ" in Lake's text (except at 6:8, where it reads "those who have denied their Christ"); it speaks of "the Son of God." In Similitude 5 a faithful slave stakes and weeds a vineyard beyond his orders and is made heir with the master's son (Shepherd of Hermas 55). The angel explains: "The slave is the Son of God" (58:2), yet he is not really in a slave's place but "in great authority and lordship"; he cleansed the people's sins "working hard and bearing much toil" and gave them the law he received from his Father (59:1-3). Then a second explanation: the Holy Spirit, who existed before and created all creation, God made to live in the flesh he wanted, which served the Spirit and was made its partner (59:5-7). In Similitude 8 the great willow is God's law, and "this law is the Son of God, preached to the ends of the earth" (69:2). Harnack read these passages as adoptionist; Schaff found the book "closely connected with catholic orthodoxy"; the Catholic Encyclopedia's John Chapman judged Hermas's ideas "rather misty and confused than definitely erroneous." The readings are set out on the chapter page of Similitude 5.6 (59).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 55:2-11; Shepherd of Hermas 58:2; Shepherd of Hermas 59:1-7; Shepherd of Hermas 69:2; Shepherd of Hermas 77:1; Philippians 2:6-11; Hebrews 1:2-3

uncommon: Adolf von Harnack called the Shepherd of Hermas the one surviving complete work that clearly expresses an adoptionist Christology.

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the Spirit who created all creation
sections.b: In Similitude 5 Hermas writes: "The Holy Spirit, who existed before, who created all creation, God made to live in flesh that he wanted" (Shepherd of Hermas 59:5). The flesh served the Spirit purely and was chosen as its partner, and "all flesh in which the Holy Spirit has lived will receive a reward, if it is found undefiled and spotless" (59:7). So the Shepherd warns: "If you defile your flesh, you will defile the Holy Spirit too" (60:2). Lake's note reads the passage as speaking of "the Son who is the Spirit," as Similitude 9 says, "that Spirit is the Son of God" (78:1). The Plain English Translation reads the Spirit that "lives in" each believer's flesh (60:1) as this same Holy Spirit, as in 1 Corinthians 6:19, though the words can also be read of the believer's own spirit; the note at Shepherd of Hermas 59:5 explains the capitals.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 59:5-7; Shepherd of Hermas 60:1-4; Shepherd of Hermas 78:1; 1 Corinthians 6:19; Genesis 1:2

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the Spirit made to live in flesh
sections.b: Hermas has no word like "became flesh" (John 1:14), but he says God made the pre-existent Holy Spirit "live in flesh that he chose," and that this flesh, after serving the Spirit well, was chosen as the Spirit's partner and given a place and a reward (Shepherd of Hermas 59:5-7). Lake explains the flesh as "the human being" in whom "the Spirit had been incarnate." Readers differ on whether this is an incarnation of a pre-existent divine Son (Schaff) or the adoption of a chosen man in whom the Spirit lived (Harnack). Hermas also insists against those who despised the body that flesh and spirit "belong together" (60:4).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 59:5-7; Shepherd of Hermas 60:1-4; John 1:14; Philippians 2:7; Romans 1:3-4

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: Father, Son, Spirit and angels
sections.b: Similitude 5 has God the Creator, his Son, the Holy Spirit who "created all creation," and the glorious angels whom God takes as advisers (Shepherd of Hermas 59:4-7). The relation of the Son and the Spirit is unclear: Lake's note speaks of "the Son who is the Spirit," and one Latin version adds at 58:2, "but the Son is the Holy Spirit." Lake judges that Hermas's Christology is "very hard to reconstruct." For historians of doctrine the book shows how Roman Christians spoke before the language of later creeds was settled.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 58:2; Shepherd of Hermas 59:4-7; Shepherd of Hermas 69:3; Shepherd of Hermas 78:1; Matthew 28:19

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: Michael over the church
sections.b: In Similitude 8 a tall, glorious angel cuts sticks from a great willow and gives one to each believer, then checks them (Shepherd of Hermas 67). The Shepherd explains: "The great and glorious angel is Michael, who has authority over this people and steers them. For he is the one who puts the law into the hearts of those who believe" (69:3). Hermas gives the church's angel the office Michael has over Israel in Daniel 12:1 and in 1 Enoch 20:5 ("in charge of the people"), and the work of Jeremiah 31:33 (the law on the heart). Since in Similitude 9 a glorious figure is the Son of God, Lake says that this, with what Similitude 9 says of the Son and the Spirit, makes Hermas's Christology "very hard to reconstruct"; Harnack calls it "not certain" whether Hermas identifies the Son with the chief archangel.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 67:2; Shepherd of Hermas 69:3-5; Daniel 12:1; Daniel 10:21; 1 Enoch 20:5; Jeremiah 31:33; Jude 1:9; Revelation 12:7

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: angels of luxury, punishment and the law
sections.b: The Similitudes are full of angels. The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, teaches Hermas (Shepherd of Hermas 51:1). The "holy angels who were created first" are the Lord's advisers, and the stakes of the vineyard are angels who "hold his people together" (58:3; 59:2). Similitude 6 shows two angels as shepherds: a cheerful young shepherd, "the angel of luxury and deceit," who wears out souls, and a wild one, "the angel of punishment," who is "one of the righteous angels" and drives sinners through the thorns of everyday troubles until they repent (62:1-63:6). A "glorious angel" orders Hermas's own affliction (66:1-5), and in Similitude 8 the glorious angel of the willow is Michael (69:3).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 58:3; Shepherd of Hermas 59:2; Shepherd of Hermas 62:1-63:6; Shepherd of Hermas 66:1-6; Shepherd of Hermas 69:3; Hebrews 1:14; Daniel 10:13

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: a slave made heir
sections.b: Hermas begins his book by saying he was sold as a slave to a woman named Rhoda (Shepherd of Hermas 1:1). In Similitude 5 he tells of a slave promised freedom for staking a vineyard, who does more than he was told and is made "an heir together with" the master's son; the slave then shares the master's gifts of food with his fellow slaves (55:2-11). The angel says the slave is the Son of God (58:2) and then that it is "the flesh" which "served the Spirit well as a slave" (59:5). The story uses the hopes of Roman slaves (freedom, and beyond freedom, adoption) to speak of God's reward, as Paul does in Galatians 4:7.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 1:1; Shepherd of Hermas 55:2-11; Shepherd of Hermas 58:2; Shepherd of Hermas 59:5-7; Galatians 4:1-7; Romans 8:15-17

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the elm and the vine, and the slave's vineyard
sections.b: Two of Hermas's parables use vines. In Similitude 2 a vine trained up an elm bears much fruit, while on the ground it bears little and rotten fruit; the elm, fruitless itself, holds up the vine and in drought feeds it with water. So the rich support the poor and the poor pray for the rich (Shepherd of Hermas 51). In Similitude 5 a master plants a vineyard and leaves it to a slave, who stakes it, digs it and weeds it; "the vines are this people, whom he himself planted" (58:2), the stakes are angels and the weeds are the lawless acts of God's slaves (58:3). The picture comes from Isaiah 5 and from Jesus' parable of the vineyard (Mark 12:1-9).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 51:1-10; Shepherd of Hermas 55:2-5; Shepherd of Hermas 58:2-3; Isaiah 5:1-7; Mark 12:1-9

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: two cities, two laws
sections.b: The first Similitude makes Christians foreigners in a city whose lord can throw them out for not keeping his laws; their own city, with its own law, is far away. Whoever buys fields and builds houses here cannot go home, and whoever denies his own law to keep them will be shut out of his city (Shepherd of Hermas 50:1-5). So: "Since you live in a foreign land, get nothing more ready for yourself than what is enough for you to live on" (50:6), and spend the rest on the poor (50:8). Lake's note points to Hebrews 13:14.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 50:1-11; Hebrews 13:14; Hebrews 11:13-16; 1 Peter 2:11; Philippians 3:20

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the willow that loves life
sections.b: Similitude 8 is a picture of a church given time to repent. Each believer receives a stick from a great willow, God's law; when the sticks are returned, many are dry, cracked or half dead. The Shepherd plants them all and waters them, because the willow "loves life" and its Creator "wants all who received branches from this tree to live" (Shepherd of Hermas 68:6-9). Days later many sticks have turned green and even bear fruit (70-71). The explanation names each group: apostates and betrayers, who did not repent; hypocrites and false teachers who would not let sinners repent, many of whom did; the double-minded, the quarrelsome, those tangled in business, those who denied, the rich who lived with the pagans. For most, repentance is still open if it is quick (72-76). "Repenting of sins brings life, but not repenting brings death" (72:6). Similitude 7 adds that forgiveness is not "at once": the penitent must humble himself and bear suffering before God's healing (66:4-5).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 66:4-5; Shepherd of Hermas 68:6-9; Shepherd of Hermas 72:1-6; Shepherd of Hermas 73:1-6; Shepherd of Hermas 77:1-4; 2 Peter 3:9; Acts 11:18

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: affliction after repentance (Similitudes 6-8)
sections.b: Similitude 6 shows "the angel of punishment," a righteous angel who drives those who wandered into the thorns of everyday troubles (losses, need, sickness, insults) until they repent and are handed over to the angel of repentance "for good training" (Shepherd of Hermas 63:2-6). In Similitude 7 Hermas, whose household has repented, is told: "So do you think the sins of those who repent are forgiven at once? Not at all. The one who repents must torment his own soul, be firmly humble in everything he does, and be afflicted with all kinds of suffering"; then God "will surely have compassion and give him some healing" (66:4). Lake sees in the book "the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance." Similitude 8 speaks of believers who "received the seal, and broke it" receiving a seal again from the angel (72:3).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 63:2-6; Shepherd of Hermas 66:2-6; Shepherd of Hermas 72:3; Shepherd of Hermas 77:3; Hebrews 12:5-11; 2 Corinthians 7:10-11

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: palm crowns for those who suffered for the law
sections.b: In Similitude 8 those whose sticks bear shoots and fruit are crowned with crowns "as if they were made of palm leaves" and sent into the tower (Shepherd of Hermas 68:1). They are those who "wrestled with the devil and defeated him ... the ones who suffered for the law" (69:6); Lake's note: "'Suffer' means 'suffer a death of martyrdom'." A second group, "afflicted for the law, but did not suffer, and did not deny," receive seals (68:2; 69:7). The picture is close to Revelation 7:9-14 (white robes and palm branches).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 68:1-3; Shepherd of Hermas 69:6-7; Revelation 7:9-14; Revelation 2:10; Ephesians 6:12

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the law that is the Son of God
sections.b: The Son "gave them the law that he received from his Father" (Shepherd of Hermas 59:3), and in Similitude 8 the great willow over all the earth "is God's law, which was given to the whole world. And this law is the Son of God, preached to the ends of the earth" (69:2). Lake notes that here "the law means the Christian rule of life, not (as in the N.T.) the Jewish Law." Each believer's stick is the law, and its state shows whether the law was kept (69:4).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 59:3; Shepherd of Hermas 69:2-4; Galatians 6:2; Isaiah 2:3; Jeremiah 31:33

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: torments of everyday life
sections.b: The "angel of punishment" of Similitude 6 punishes with "losses, ... need, ... sicknesses of every kind, ... all kinds of unrest," and insults (Shepherd of Hermas 63:4). People blame the Lord, but when they repent they see their deeds and say "he is a righteous judge" (63:5-6). In Similitude 7 Hermas himself suffers for the sins of his household, because they cannot be afflicted unless their head is (66:3). Suffering here is training (paideia) toward repentance, as in Hebrews 12:5-11.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 63:1-6; Shepherd of Hermas 64:4; Shepherd of Hermas 66:1-7; Hebrews 12:5-11; Proverbs 3:11-12
